questions.title: Enzymes that execute apoptosis
questions.question: Apoptosis is brought by a group of enzymes called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Catalases break down hydrogen peroxide as part of the cell's antioxidant defence against oxidative stress; they play no role in executing programmed cell death.
explanations.B: Correct. Apoptosis is executed by caspases, a family of enzymes activated in a cascade once the cell commits to programmed death. Once active, caspases destroy the nuclear membrane and activate DNAases, which degrade nuclear DNA -- the ordered, energy-dependent dismantling that distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis. The bcl-2 protein family sits upstream of the caspases, controlling whether this cascade is triggered at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Caspases are technically a class of protease, but "proteases" alone is too broad an answer; the specific caspase family, not proteases in general, is what this teaching point names as apoptosis's executioner enzymes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lipases hydrolyse triglycerides and drive enzymatic fat necrosis (as in acute pancreatitis), a form of cell death unrelated to apoptosis's proteolytic execution machinery.

questions.learning_objective: Name caspases as the enzyme family that executes apoptosis.

questions.title: Bcl-2's role in cell death
questions.question: Bcl2 gene plays an important role in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inflammation is the vascular and cellular response to tissue injury or infection; the bcl-2 protein family does not regulate the inflammatory response, and apoptosis itself is characteristically non-inflammatory.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Necrosis is passive, uncontrolled cell death from severe injury, triggered by mechanisms like ATP depletion and membrane damage; bcl-2 does not control this pathway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Autolysis is the self-digestion of a dead cell by its own released lysosomal enzymes after death has already occurred, not a process bcl-2 regulates.
explanations.D: Correct. Apoptosis is controlled by the bcl-2 protein family, which sets the threshold at which the caspase cascade that executes programmed cell death is triggered. Anti-apoptotic bcl-2 family members restrain this cascade, while pro-apoptotic family members promote it, so the balance between them decides whether a given cell survives or dies by apoptosis. This regulatory role is why bcl-2 overexpression is implicated in cancers that resist normal programmed cell death, such as follicular lymphoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bcl-2 gene family controls (regulates) apoptosis.

questions.title: Enzymatic fat necrosis and acute pancreatitis
questions.question: Enzymatic fat necrosis is characteristic of :

explanations.A: Incorrect. Moist gangrene is coagulative necrosis complicated by superadded bacterial putrefaction, not the lipase-driven enzymatic fat necrosis this question describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A pyogenic abscess is a localised collection of pus, the product of liquefactive necrosis, not of pancreatic lipase acting on adipose tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tuberculous peritonitis is associated with caseation necrosis from tuberculous infection, a different mechanism from enzymatic fat necrosis.
explanations.D: Correct. Enzymatic fat necrosis occurs in acute (haemorrhagic) pancreatitis, where leaked pancreatic lipase splits mesenteric and peripancreatic fat into free fatty acids. Those fatty acids then combine with calcium to form white, chalky calcium soaps -- the macroscopic finding that gives this necrosis its name. This is distinct from traumatic fat necrosis (as in the breast), which follows direct mechanical injury to adipose tissue rather than enzyme leakage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify acute haemorrhagic pancreatitis as the classic setting for enzymatic fat necrosis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis"

questions.title: Apoptosis features (except one)
questions.question: Feature of apoptosis include all of the following except:

explanations.A: Correct. Apoptosis deletes individual cells while their membrane stays intact, so cell contents are never released into the surrounding tissue. It therefore does not provoke an inflammatory response, unlike necrosis, which spills cell contents and does inflame the surrounding tissue. This absence of inflammation is precisely why apoptosis is described as a clean, programmed way for a cell to die, in contrast to necrosis's messy, passive death.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nuclear chromatin condensation (pyknosis-like clumping of the nucleus) is a genuine, defining morphological feature of an apoptotic cell, not the exception this question asks for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Shrinkage of cell size is a genuine feature of apoptosis -- the cell actively shrinks with an intact membrane before breaking into apoptotic bodies -- not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. DNA fragmentation, driven by caspase-activated DNAases, is a genuine hallmark of apoptosis, not the exception being asked for.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that apoptosis, unlike necrosis, does not provoke inflammation because the cell membrane stays intact.

questions.title: Pulmonary infarction as a type of necrosis
questions.question: Pulmonary infarction is:

explanations.A: Correct. Pulmonary infarction, like most solid-organ infarcts (kidney, spleen, heart), follows coagulative necrosis: acute ischaemia denatures both the structural proteins and the enzymes that would digest them, so the cellular outline is held for a time even though the cells are dead. Microscopically the tissue shows loss of nuclei with increased cytoplasmic eosinophilia but a retained overall architecture -- the "ghost" of the original tissue. This is the general rule for infarcts in solid organs, with the brain as the well-known exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Liquefactive necrosis, not coagulative, is the exception seen in the brain (a lipid-rich, stroma-poor organ) and in pus, not in a typical solid-organ infarct such as the lung.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Caseation necrosis is the cheese-like necrosis specific to tuberculosis, not the pattern seen in a vascular infarct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fat necrosis (traumatic or enzymatic) occurs in adipose tissue, not in the parenchyma of an infarcted lung.

questions.learning_objective: Classify pulmonary infarction as coagulative necrosis, the pattern typical of solid-organ infarcts.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Coagulative necrosis"

questions.title: Nuclear changes in necrosis (except one)
questions.question: The following nuclear changes can be seen in necrotic cells except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Karyorrhexis -- destructive fragmentation of the nucleus, typically following pyknosis -- is one of the three genuine nuclear changes of necrosis, not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pyknosis -- shrinkage of the nucleus into a small, dense, deeply basophilic mass -- is a genuine early nuclear change of necrosis, not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Karyolysis -- fading of nuclear basophilia until the nucleus disappears completely -- is a genuine nuclear change of necrosis, not the exception.
explanations.D: Correct. The nucleus of a necrotic cell shrinks (pyknosis), fragments (karyorrhexis) and fades away (karyolysis) -- it never enlarges. "Nuclear enlargement" describes no recognised step of necrosis and is the exception this question asks for. Eventually the nucleus disappears completely, while the cytoplasm becomes more eosinophilic from denatured protein and loss of RNA.

questions.learning_objective: List karyolysis, pyknosis and karyorrhexis as the three nuclear changes of necrosis, and reject nuclear enlargement as none of them.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Nuclear enlargement"

questions.title: Necrosis type in tuberculosis
questions.question: Type of necrosis present in tuberculosis:

explanations.A: Correct. Caseation necrosis is the necrosis of tuberculosis: the necrotic tissue appears semi-solid, yellowish and cheese-like (from casein), and under the microscope shows granular, structureless pink material with the tissue architecture completely lost. It occurs through digestion of tissue by activated macrophages, and lipids liberated from the tubercle bacillus's capsule add to the cheese-like appearance. This total loss of architecture is what distinguishes it from coagulative necrosis, the other necrosis type that stays grossly firm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fat necrosis (traumatic or enzymatic) occurs in adipose tissue -- the breast or the peripancreatic fat, for example -- not as the characteristic necrosis of tuberculous granulomas.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Liquefactive necrosis occurs in the brain and in pyogenic abscesses, not as the hallmark necrosis of tuberculosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coagulative necrosis is the necrosis of solid-organ ischaemic infarcts and retains a "ghost" tissue architecture, unlike caseation necrosis, where the architecture is completely lost.

questions.learning_objective: Identify caseation necrosis as the necrosis type characteristic of tuberculosis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Caseation necrosis"

questions.title: Definition of karyorrhexis
questions.question: Which of the following describes Karyorrhexis:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Lysis of chromatin" describes karyolysis -- the fading of nuclear basophilia until the nucleus disappears -- a different, later nuclear change from karyorrhexis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Condensed chromatin" describes pyknosis, the nuclear shrinkage into a dense, deeply staining mass that precedes karyorrhexis, not karyorrhexis itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Shrinkage of chromatin" is again pyknosis's defining feature, not karyorrhexis's -- the two terms are commonly confused precisely because pyknosis is followed immediately by karyorrhexis.
explanations.D: Correct. Karyorrhexis is destructive fragmentation of the nucleus into small pieces, following pyknosis in the sequence of nuclear changes seen in necrosis. It is one of the three named nuclear changes -- karyolysis, pyknosis and karyorrhexis -- and the fragmentation, not shrinkage or fading, is the specific feature the name records. Confusing karyorrhexis with pyknosis (shrinkage) is the classic pitfall this question tests.

questions.learning_objective: Define karyorrhexis as nuclear fragmentation, distinct from pyknosis (shrinkage) and karyolysis (fading/lysis).

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Fragmented chromatin"

questions.title: Liquefactive necrosis in cerebral infarction
questions.question: Liqufactive necrosis is seen in

explanations.A: Incorrect. Malignant hypertension is associated with fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles, not liquefactive necrosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pulmonary tuberculosis is associated with caseation necrosis, the cheese-like necrosis of mycobacterial infection, not liquefactive necrosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Kidney infarction, like most solid-organ infarcts, undergoes coagulative necrosis, retaining the tissue outline -- the opposite pattern from liquefactive necrosis.
explanations.D: Correct. Liquefactive (colliquative) necrosis occurs in central nervous system infarction, because the brain is rich in lipid, soft, and lacks the supporting stromal framework that keeps other infarcted organs firm; the dead tissue turns to fluid and the area is later walled off by glial tissue into a cyst. The other classic example of liquefactive necrosis is pus, in suppurative (pyogenic) inflammation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cerebral (CNS) infarction as the classic organ setting for liquefactive necrosis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Cerebral infarction"

questions.title: Cellular swelling / fatty change is reversible
questions.question: Cellular swelling of fatty change is an example of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neoplastic transformation is a permanent, heritable change toward a tumour phenotype, not a description of the reversible morphological changes of early cell injury.
explanations.B: Correct. Cellular (cloudy) swelling and fatty change are both patterns of reversible cell injury: cloudy swelling is the earliest change, from loss of the sodium pump and accumulation of sodium and water, followed by hydropic change, and then fatty change, in which lipid accumulates as vacuoles in cells that handle fat. If the injurious stimulus is removed at this stage, the cell can recover.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Necrosis is irreversible cell death, the endpoint injury progresses to if it is not removed -- the opposite of the reversible pattern this question describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Apoptosis is a distinct, energy-dependent programmed cell death pathway, not a description of cellular swelling or fatty change.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Dysplastic change describes disordered, pre-neoplastic cellular maturation, not the reversible accumulation of water or lipid seen in early cell injury.

questions.topic: Cellular accumulations: cloudy swelling, hydropic degeneration and fatty changes
questions.learning_objective: Classify cellular swelling and fatty change as patterns of reversible cell injury.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Reversible injury"

questions.module_subject: AUN-MPT-104 > Pathology > Cellular Response to Injury > Reversible injury

questions.title: What cloudy swelling accumulates
questions.question: Cloudy swelling is characterized by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The liver is one of the classic sites of cloudy swelling, along with myocardial and renal tubular cells, so it is commonly, not rarely, involved.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cloudy swelling affects parenchymal (epithelial) cells such as hepatocytes, myocardial cells and renal tubular cells, not fibrous (connective) tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cloudy swelling is the earliest and mildest pattern of reversible injury, not an irreversible one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fat accumulation describes fatty change, a later and distinct pattern of reversible injury from cloudy swelling.
explanations.E: Correct. Cloudy swelling is one of the earliest changes of cell injury: loss of the sodium pump lets sodium and water accumulate inside the cell, so it swells and the cytoplasm looks granular under the microscope. It is seen classically in liver, myocardial and renal tubular cells, and it precedes the more advanced hydropic (vacuolar) change and then fatty change if the injury continues.

questions.topic: Cellular accumulations: cloudy swelling, hydropic degeneration and fatty changes
questions.learning_objective: State that cloudy swelling is water (not fat) accumulating inside injured cells.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Water accumulation in cells"

questions.title: Microscopic appearance of the fatty liver
questions.question: Liver affected by fatty change is characterized by:

options.A: Shows the presence of multiple granulomas
options.C: Shows bile accumulation in bile canaliculi
options.E: Fat vacuoles stained esinophilic on H&E stained sections

explanations.A: Incorrect. Multiple granulomas are a feature of granulomatous disease (such as tuberculosis or sarcoidosis), not of simple hepatic fatty change.
explanations.B: Correct. In fatty change, small intracytoplasmic droplets or large vacuoles of fat accumulate in liver cells, and the nucleus is flattened and pushed to one side of the cell -- giving the hepatocyte a signet-ring appearance, the same shape seen in the mucin-filled cells of signet-ring cell carcinoma, but here from fat rather than mucin. Grossly, the fatty liver is enlarged and soft with rounded borders, and its cut section is yellow and greasy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bile accumulation in bile canaliculi describes cholestasis, a different process from fatty change, though both can occur in liver disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fatty liver is soft, not hard, in consistency -- its softness is part of why its borders become rounded.
explanations.E: Incorrect. On a routine paraffin section the fat vacuole appears empty, not eosinophilic, because the lipid dissolves out in the xylol and alcohol used during tissue processing.

questions.topic: Cellular accumulations: cloudy swelling, hydropic degeneration and fatty changes
questions.learning_objective: Describe the signet-ring hepatocyte appearance of fatty change and its cause (a fat vacuole displacing the nucleus).

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Shows signet ring cells"

questions.title: The tigered (tabby cat) heart
questions.question: Tigered effect of heart is seen in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amyloid infiltration makes the heart firm and waxy, not the streaked "tigered" appearance this question describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cloudy swelling is a microscopic finding (granular cytoplasm from water accumulation), not the gross, striped appearance named here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hydropic change is a microscopic vacuolar finding, not a gross tigering pattern of the heart.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyaline change gives a glassy pink appearance on microscopy, not the gross striped pattern of a tigered heart.
explanations.E: Correct. Fatty change of the myocardium can be spotty, in ischaemia, or diffuse, in toxaemia such as diphtheria; the spotty pattern gives the gross "tabby cat" or "tigered" heart, in which the columnae carneae show brown dots (unaffected muscle) alternating with yellow ones (fat-laden muscle). This is one lesion unevenly distributed, not two separate lesions.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the tigered/tabby cat heart as the gross appearance of spotty myocardial fatty change.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Fatty change"

questions.title: Hepatic steatosis and progression to fibrosis
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true for hepatic steatosis:

explanations.A: Correct. Hepatic steatosis (fatty change) arises from excess fatty acid entry, decreased fatty acid oxidation, increased triglyceride formation, or impaired lipoprotein export -- alcohol drives two of these routes at once, which is why it is such a heavy cause. If the underlying insult (such as continued alcohol use) persists, this reversible accumulation can progress through steatohepatitis to hepatic fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Simple fatty change is a reversible accumulation, not "always irreversible" -- removing the cause (such as stopping alcohol) allows the liver to recover before fibrosis develops.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alcohol is one of the most important and well-established causes of hepatic steatosis, acting by increasing triglyceride formation and impairing lipoprotein secretion, so steatosis is very much associated with alcohol intake.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Steatosis does not "mostly" proceed to hepatocellular carcinoma; most cases either resolve or, if the insult persists, progress through fibrosis rather than going directly and predominantly to malignancy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Steatosis is reversible only while the underlying cause is removed early; sustained injury can progress it toward fibrosis, so "always reversible" overstates the natural history.

questions.topic: Cellular accumulations: cloudy swelling, hydropic degeneration and fatty changes
questions.learning_objective: State that hepatic steatosis, if the underlying cause persists, can progress toward hepatic fibrosis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: May progress to hepatic fibrosis"

questions.title: Amyloidosis associated with multiple myeloma
questions.question: Amyloidosis is commonly associated with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Pursitis" is not a recognised amyloidosis-associated condition in this teaching set.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chronic otitis media is a middle-ear infection, not one of the diseases classically associated with amyloid deposition.
explanations.C: Correct. Primary (myeloma-associated) systemic amyloidosis deposits AL protein and accompanies multiple myeloma, a plasma-cell bone-marrow tumour that produces a large amount of one immunoglobulin light-chain type; that light chain is what forms the amyloid fibril. This is distinct from secondary (reactive) amyloidosis, which deposits AA protein and follows long-standing chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or tuberculosis instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Congestive heart failure can be a consequence of cardiac amyloid deposition, but it is not itself a cause or association that produces amyloidosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Acute osteomyelitis is an acute bacterial bone infection; secondary amyloidosis follows chronic, long-standing inflammatory conditions, not an acute infective process.

questions.learning_objective: Identify multiple myeloma as the classic association of primary (AL) systemic amyloidosis.

questions.title: What dystrophic calcification is associated with
questions.question: Dystrophic calcification is most commonly associated with

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased work load alone does not explain dystrophic calcification; the calcium is deposited because the local tissue is already damaged, not because it is working harder.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diminished blood supply can cause the necrosis that then calcifies, but it is the resulting tissue damage, not the ischaemia itself, that is the direct association tested here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chronic irritation is not the specific association named for dystrophic calcification in this teaching set; the defining feature is pre-existing tissue damage, of which necrosis is the clearest example.
explanations.D: Correct. Dystrophic calcification occurs in tissue already affected by disease -- with a normal serum calcium level -- through local precipitation of insoluble calcium salts. Classic examples are areas of necrosis such as old tuberculous (caseous) lesions, fat necrosis, old thrombi, and atheromatous plaques: the common thread is damaged or dead tissue, not a high blood calcium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is the hallmark of metastatic, not dystrophic, calcification -- dystrophic calcification specifically occurs at a normal serum calcium level.

questions.learning_objective: Associate dystrophic calcification with pre-existing damaged/necrotic tissue at a normal serum calcium.

questions.title: Site of amyloid deposition in the kidney
questions.question: In renal amyloidosis, which of the following is a site of amyloid deposition?

explanations.A: Correct. In renal amyloidosis, amyloid is deposited in the basement membrane of the glomerular capillaries and mesangium, and also in the tubular basement membrane, where it appears as a thick, homogeneous pink material on microscopy. As deposition progresses the glomerular capillaries become obliterated by amyloid, arteriolar walls thicken causing ischaemia and tubular atrophy, and the patient presents clinically with proteinuria followed by renal failure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The renal pelvis is the urine-collecting cavity of the kidney, not a site where amyloid is deposited within the renal parenchyma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The renal capsule is the kidney's fibrous outer covering, not a site of amyloid deposition, which occurs within the glomerular and tubular basement membranes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ureter is a separate structure conveying urine from the kidney to the bladder, not a described site of renal amyloid deposition.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Perinephric fat surrounds the kidney but is not a site where amyloid is deposited in renal amyloidosis, which targets basement membranes within the kidney itself.

questions.topic: Cellular accumulations: Amyloidosis, hyalinosis and pathological calcification
questions.learning_objective: Localise renal amyloid deposition to the glomerular and tubular basement membranes.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Basement membrane of collecting tubules"

questions.title: Metastatic calcification and diffuse skeletal metastasis
questions.question: Which is true regarding metastatic calcification:

options.B: Due to increased phosphatase activity of the tissues
options.D: Calcium is deposited on necrotic tissue
options.E: May occurs in patients with diffuse skeletal metastasis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Metastatic calcification occurs specifically because the serum calcium level is high (hypercalcaemia), not normal -- a normal serum calcium is the hallmark of dystrophic, not metastatic, calcification.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased tissue phosphatase activity is not the mechanism named for metastatic calcification; the driver is a raised blood calcium level reaching otherwise-viable tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Serum calcium is high, not low, in metastatic calcification -- a low serum calcium would not drive calcium salts to precipitate in tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deposition on necrotic (already-damaged) tissue at a normal serum calcium describes dystrophic calcification; metastatic calcification instead deposits in viable, healthy tissue because the blood calcium level itself is elevated.
explanations.E: Correct. Metastatic calcification occurs in viable tissues whenever there is hypercalcaemia, and diffuse skeletal metastasis (such as from breast cancer) is one of its recognised causes, through the bone destruction it produces. Other causes include elevated parathyroid hormone, hypervitaminosis D, and Paget's disease; the deposits sit in gastric mucosa, kidney, lungs and blood vessel walls, usually without clinical dysfunction unless the kidney is heavily affected (nephrocalcinosis).

questions.title: Zenker's degeneration as hyaline change
questions.question: Zenker's degeneration is an example of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hydropic change is water accumulation giving a pale, vacuolated cytoplasm, a different appearance from the glassy pink change named here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fatty change is lipid accumulation as cytoplasmic vacuoles, not the homogeneous pink appearance Zenker's degeneration describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cloudy swelling is granular cytoplasmic swelling from water accumulation, not a glassy pink hyaline appearance.
explanations.D: Correct. "Hyaline" names a homogeneous, glassy, pink appearance on routine H&E staining rather than one specific substance. Zenker's (waxy) degeneration is hyaline change in skeletal muscle, classically described in the rectus abdominis in severe infections such as typhoid fever, and it sits alongside other hyaline-change examples such as Russell bodies, Mallory hyaline and arteriolar hyalinosis -- different substances that all happen to look alike under the microscope.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Amyloidosis is extracellular beta-pleated protein deposition, a specific and distinct entity from the broader descriptive category of hyaline change, even though amyloid can also look glassy pink.
